title: SSH Connection Refused or Timeout
desc: Cannot connect via SSH — connection refused, timeout, or permission denied.

steps.text: Check if SSH service is running on the target
steps.note: Should show active (running). If not: systemctl start sshd

steps.text: Confirm SSH is listening on the expected port
steps.note: No output means SSH isn't bound to that port — check /etc/ssh/sshd_config

steps.text: Check firewall isn't blocking SSH
steps.note: Port 22 or custom SSH port must be ALLOW IN

steps.text: Test from the target server itself
steps.note: If this works but remote doesn't, problem is network/firewall between hosts

steps.text: Check /var/log/auth.log for rejection reason
steps.note: Look for "refused connect", "invalid user", "publickey" failures

steps.text: Verify the SSH port in config
steps.note: Default is 22 — if changed, clients must specify: ssh -p PORT user@host

title: Disk Full — System or Service Fails
desc: Server stops writing logs, services crash, or "no space left on device" errors appear.

steps.text: Confirm which partition is full
steps.note: Look for 100% Use% — note which mount point

steps.text: Check inode exhaustion too (can cause same symptoms)
steps.note: IUse% at 100% = inode exhaustion even with free disk space

steps.text: Find the largest directories
steps.note: Identifies top-level space consumers

steps.text: Drill down into the biggest offender
steps.note: Repeat at each level until you find the culprit

steps.text: Check for large log files
steps.note: Log files over 100MB are common culprits

steps.text: Check for deleted files still held open by processes
steps.cmd: lsof | grep deleted | awk '{print $7, $1}' | sort -rn | head
steps.note: A process holding a deleted file keeps the space allocated — restart that process to free it

title: High CPU Usage — System Slow or Unresponsive
desc: Server load is high, applications are slow, CPU at near 100%.

steps.text: Identify the top CPU consumers
steps.note: Top of list is your culprit — note PID and process name

steps.text: Get live view with thread-level detail
steps.note: Press F6 to sort by CPU, H to show threads, t for tree view

steps.text: Check system load average vs CPU count
steps.note: Load > number of CPUs = overloaded. 4 CPUs with load 8.0 = severely overloaded

steps.text: Check if it's I/O wait (not pure CPU)
steps.note: High %iowait means disk is the bottleneck, not the CPU itself

steps.text: Check for zombie processes (can accumulate)
steps.note: Zombies don't consume CPU but indicate a parent process not cleaning up children

steps.text: If a process is runaway, check what it's doing
steps.note: Shows system calls — helps diagnose infinite loops or stuck operations

title: Windows — No Network Connectivity
desc: Windows machine cannot reach the network, internet, or specific hosts.

steps.text: Check adapter status and IP address
steps.note: Look for 169.254.x.x (APIPA) = DHCP failed. No IP = adapter problem.

steps.text: Flush DNS cache and renew IP
steps.note: Fixes stale DNS and DHCP issues. Run as admin.

steps.text: Test loopback (local TCP stack)
steps.note: If this fails, TCP/IP stack is broken — netsh int ip reset

steps.text: Test gateway reachability
steps.note: Get gateway from ipconfig. If unreachable: cable, switch, or adapter issue

steps.text: Test external DNS
steps.note: If this works but domain names don't: DNS issue, not routing

steps.text: Reset TCP/IP and Winsock if all else fails
steps.cmd: netsh int ip reset && netsh winsock reset
steps.note: Requires reboot. Resets entire network stack to defaults.

title: Port Already in Use — Service Won't Start
desc: A service fails to start because its port is already bound by another process.

steps.text: Find which process is using the port (Linux)
steps.note: Replace PORT with the number. Shows PID and process name.

steps.text: Find which process is using the port (Windows)
steps.note: Note the PID in the last column, then use tasklist to identify it

steps.text: Identify the process name from PID
steps.note: Get a human-readable name from the PID shown in step 1

steps.text: Decide: kill or reconfigure
steps.note: If the process shouldn't be there, kill it. If it's a duplicate of your service, stop it via systemctl first.

steps.text: Prevent recurrence — check what starts that process
steps.note: If the process is a service that shouldn't run, disable it: systemctl disable name

title: Windows Service Fails to Start
desc: A Windows service shows Stopped or fails immediately on start — Error 1053, 1067, etc.

steps.text: Check service configuration and exe path
steps.note: Verify the BINARY_PATH_NAME exists and is correct. Wrong path = immediate failure.

steps.text: Try starting and get the exact error
steps.note: Note the error code: 1053 = didn't respond, 1067 = process terminated unexpectedly

steps.text: Check Application Event Log for details
steps.note: Error details are usually here with the exact exception or missing dependency

steps.text: Check if the service account has correct permissions
steps.note: Check LOG_ON_AS — if it's a domain account, verify password hasn't changed

steps.text: Check for dependency services
steps.note: If a dependency service is stopped, this one will fail. Start dependencies first.
